title: How a small shop owner takes payments and chases unpaid invoices
candidateBrief: You are doing discovery interviews about how very small businesses get paid. Priya runs a two-person picture framing shop. You have 12 minutes. You are not allowed to describe anything you are building. Find out what she actually does today, on specific recent occasions, and what the problem has already cost her.

patient.name: Priya
patient.persona: Runs a picture framing shop with one employee. Busy, friendly, slightly impatient. Talks about her work in concrete terms and does not use business jargon. Plays down problems at first: her instinct is to say things are fine and that she has a system. Will give details when asked about a particular occasion, but answers a general question with a general answer.
patient.openingLine: Hi, yes, come in. Sorry about the mess, we are mid-order. What did you want to know?

rubric.label: Explains who you are and what the session is for
rubric.exampleQuestion: Thanks for the time. I'm trying to understand how you get paid at the moment, not to show you anything.

rubric.label: Says it is voluntary, and agrees recording before starting
rubric.exampleQuestion: Is it alright if I take notes? You can stop at any point, or skip anything.

rubric.label: Opens on their world, not on your idea
rubric.exampleQuestion: How do you handle getting paid at the moment?

rubric.label: Asks about a specific recent occasion
rubric.exampleQuestion: When did an invoice last go unpaid? Tell me about that one.

rubric.label: Has them walk through what they actually did
rubric.exampleQuestion: What did you do first when you noticed, and then what?

rubric.label: Finds what they already do about it
rubric.exampleQuestion: What do you do about it today?

rubric.label: Finds what the problem has already cost them
rubric.exampleQuestion: Have you tried anything to fix it, or spent anything on it?

rubric.label: Establishes who else is involved
rubric.exampleQuestion: Who else is part of this?

rubric.label: Asks about an occasion when it went wrong
rubric.exampleQuestion: When did it last go wrong?

rubric.label: Follows something they clearly felt strongly about
rubric.exampleQuestion: That sounded like it annoyed you. What was that like?

rubric.label: Lets them say what matters most, unprompted
rubric.exampleQuestion: Of everything you have told me, what gets in your way most?

rubric.label: Asks what you did not think to ask
rubric.exampleQuestion: Is there anything I should have asked and did not?

rubric.label: Says what happens next with what they told you
rubric.exampleQuestion: I'll write this up for the team; nothing goes out with your name on it.

facts.text: Most customers pay by card in the shop. Businesses that order framing in bulk get an invoice, and those are the ones that go unpaid.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: a small business owner describing how she is paid.

facts.text: A design studio owes her for three jobs from February. It is about 1,900 pounds. She has chased it four times.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: a specific unpaid invoice, which only surfaces when the interviewer asks about a particular occasion.

facts.text: She emailed, then rang and got voicemail, then emailed again with the invoice attached, then left it because she did not want to lose the account.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: the actual sequence of what she did, which a general question never reaches.

facts.text: She keeps a paper list by the till and rewrites it every Monday. Her employee does not use it.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: the existing workaround, which is the strongest signal in a discovery interview.

facts.text: She paid an accountant 300 pounds last year to chase two invoices, and got one of them. She reckons she spends most of a Monday morning on it.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: money and time already spent, the evidence that the problem is real rather than merely agreed to be annoying.

facts.text: Her employee Marek takes orders when she is out, and writes them on whatever is nearest.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: the second person involved, who never comes up unless asked about.

facts.text: In the spring she framed a large order on a verbal go-ahead and the customer changed their mind. She kept the frames and could not sell them.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: an occasion when it went wrong, reached only by asking for one.

facts.text: What actually bothers her is having to ask. She says chasing money makes her feel like she is begging, and she would rather write it off than ring a third time.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: the reason behind the behaviour, which comes out only when the interviewer follows the feeling rather than the facts.

facts.text: Asked what gets in her way most, she says it is not the money. It is not knowing, on any given day, who owes her what.

source.quote: Authored for this repository as synthetic practice content: her own priority, which differs from the one an interviewer would have guessed.
